opus-5.5.text:
Sure. The basic idea is surprisingly old: it's triangulation, the same geometry surveyors have used for centuries.

You have two things separated by a known distance: a projector and a camera. The projector shines a known pattern of light onto the scene. That could be a stripe, a grid, a set of dots, or a sequence of black-and-white bars. The camera, sitting off to the side, looks at how that pattern lands on the objects in front of it.

The key is that the pattern deforms depending on the shape of what it hits. If you project a straight line of light onto a flat table, the camera sees a straight line. Put a coffee mug in the way, and from the camera's angle that line bends and shifts. How far it shifts tells you how far away the surface is.

To make that precise, you need to solve what we call the correspondence problem. For any bright spot the camera sees, you have to know which ray of light from the projector produced it. Once you know that, you have two rays: one leaving the projector, one entering the camera. You know the baseline between them and both angles. So you have a triangle, and the point in space is where those two rays intersect. Do that for every pixel and you get a depth map, a cloud of 3D points.

The cleverness is mostly in designing patterns that make correspondence easy. One classic approach projects a series of binary stripe patterns, so each column of the projector gets a unique on-off code over time. Another, used in the original Microsoft Kinect, projects a pseudo-random infrared dot pattern, so each small neighborhood of dots is distinctive and can be identified in a single frame.

It has limits, and those matter a lot in robotics. Shiny surfaces reflect the pattern away, transparent objects like glasses let it pass through, and bright sunlight can wash it out. That's one reason robots still struggle to grasp things like clear plastic bottles, and why we've been combining depth sensing with learning methods that can fill in what the sensor misses.

r001.rationale: The response explains that a known projected pattern shifts or deforms on scene surfaces, and that this distortion is used with projector-camera geometry to locate 3D points.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. So the basic idea goes back to something very old, which is triangulation. If you know the positions of two points and you can measure the angles to a third point from each of them, you can compute where that third point is. Surveyors have done this for centuries.

Stereo vision does this with two cameras. You find the same feature in both images, and the difference in where it appears, the disparity, tells you how far away it is. The problem is that this requires finding corresponding points, and on a blank white wall or a shiny metal surface there's nothing to match. So you get holes in your depth map exactly where it matters most for a robot.

Structured light replaces one of the cameras with a projector. The projector throws a known pattern onto the scene, often a pseudo-random speckle of infrared dots, or a sequence of stripes. Now you don't need the scene to have texture, because you've painted texture onto it. The camera, which is offset from the projector by a known baseline, sees where those dots land. Each dot was emitted along a known ray from the projector. The camera sees it along another known ray. Those two rays intersect at exactly one point in space, and that's where the surface is.

What makes this work in practice is the pattern design. If every dot looked identical you'd have the same matching problem, so the pattern is arranged so that any small neighborhood of dots is unique. The camera can look at a patch, identify which part of the projected pattern it's seeing, and then the geometry does the rest. Do that for every pixel and you get a dense point cloud in a fraction of a second.

The original Kinect worked this way, and that was a turning point for robotics. Suddenly you had a few-hundred-dollar sensor giving you 3D data that used to cost tens of thousands. It has limits. Sunlight washes out the infrared pattern, and transparent or very dark objects absorb or pass the light so you get dropouts. That's one reason we've spent a lot of time in my lab on grasping transparent and reflective objects. But as a way to turn light into geometry, it's elegant, and it's been enormously influential.

r001.rationale: The response explains that a projector casts a known pattern and the camera uses where its dots appear on the scene, together with the known geometry, to locate surface points in space.

astra-6.text:
The basic idea is triangulation. Imagine a camera and a projector sitting a known distance apart, both looking at the same scene. The projector shines a pattern onto the objects—perhaps a series of stripes—and the camera observes where those stripes appear.

If we can identify a particular stripe in the camera image, we know two things: the direction from the projector that the light traveled, and the direction from the camera toward the point where it landed. With those directions and the known geometry of the camera and projector, we can calculate the point’s position in three-dimensional space.

The clever part is designing the patterns so you can reliably tell which projected stripe you’re seeing. You do that across the image, and you get a dense collection of points describing the surfaces in front of you.

r001.rationale: It explains that the camera locates a projected stripe in the image and combines its observed direction with the projector-camera geometry to calculate the point’s 3D position. This communicates inferring position from how the projected pattern appears on the scene.

sol-6.1.text:
The basic idea is triangulation. Imagine a camera and a projector sitting a known distance apart. The projector shines a known pattern onto the scene—perhaps a series of stripes—and the camera observes where those stripes appear on the surfaces of objects.

For a point you see in the camera, you want to identify which part of the projected pattern illuminated it. Once you know that, you have two directions: a ray from the camera and a ray from the projector. Given their positions and orientations, you can calculate where those rays intersect, and that gives you the point’s location in three dimensions.

The trick is making the pattern distinctive enough that you can reliably match what the camera sees to what the projector sent out. Do that for many points, and you get a depth map of the scene.

r001.rationale: It explains that a known projected pattern is observed on scene surfaces and matched to triangulate points’ 3D locations.
